ai-c6608a9a56.headline: Tech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reports
ai-c6608a9a56.fulltext:
A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies drove US markets down by hundreds of billions of dollars Friday. In total, the decline has knocked nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
The S&P 500, the index of the 500 most valuable companies in the US, fell by more than 1% Friday, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. It was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the same month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell less.
More than $2tn in market value is set to be wiped from the Nasdaq 100 this month, as big tech earnings intensified investor scrutiny of whether the billions being poured into artificial intelligence can generate returns quickly enough.
The wipeout would amount to slightly more than SpaceX’s entire market value. The index has fallen more than 5.8% so far in October as the AI trade ran into turbulence, with hyperscalers Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon raising spending forecasts further as they race to expand AI infrastructure.
Intel tumbled nearly 30% and is flirting with its worst day since 1974, even though the chipmaker reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell far short of analysts’ expectations.
Amazon fell 1.8% after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. The company also disclosed that it had spent more this year than anticipated.
A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12%, wiping $500bn from its market capitalization, to its worst day on record after telling investors that it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring because of similar, mammoth investments in AI.
Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make AI investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI datacenters have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward.
Such losses overshadowed an otherwise mixed day for the rest of Wall Street, with the S&P 500 roughly evenly split between gainers and losers.
Expectations are high broadly for US companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

deep-tech-9ef714d908.headline: Isro’s GSLV-F18/NVS-03 mission successful: Next-generation navigation satellite placed in orbit; NavIC co
deep-tech-9ef714d908.fulltext:
It was the 20th flight of the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle. (Photo by C Suresh Kumar)
SRIHARIKOTA: India's regional satellite navigation system, NavIC, which was facing a shortage of operational satellites, got a boost with the successful launch of NVS-03 on the intervening night of Friday and Saturday by Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro).GSLV-F18 carrying 2,250kg next-generation navigation satellite -- NVS-03 -- lifted off from the second launch pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) in Sriharikota at 11.51pm on Friday, as scheduled. It was the 20th flight of the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV). Around 18 minutes later, NVS-03 satellite was placed in a geosynchronous transfer orbit (GTO) of 37,023km apogee and 170km perigee."The rocket has successfully and precisely placed the satellite into its intended elliptical orbit. It achieved a 170km perigee and 38,080km apogee. This is the 5th mission from Sriharikota this year. GSLV has carried 34 tonnes of spacecraft to space so far. We achieved this mission with a turnaround time of just 56 days after the GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission in September. With this launch, we have restored NavIC constellation operation as we need a minimum of four satellites to perform positioning, navigation and timing services," said Isro chairman V Narayanan.
He said, “The satellite is healthy, and the solar panel has been deployed. Already three pyro walls are operated, and we have lifted. Every system is totally healthy, and we are going to continue the operation and place the satellite in the intended circular orbit.”NVS-03 is the third satellite in Isro's next-generation navigation satellite system, designed to ensure continuity of services under the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS), operationally known as NavIC. The satellite carries an indigenously developed atomic clock along with procured atomic clocks. It also carries the L1 frequency signal in addition to the existing L5 and S-band signals.NavIC is India's independent regional satellite navigation system, designed to provide positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) services across the country and an area extending approximately 1,500km beyond the Indian landmass. The additional L1 signal, alongside the existing signals, is expected to improve compatibility with other satellite navigation systems and widen the potential use of NavIC in civilian applications.The NVS-03 mission is part of Isro's plan to deploy five second-generation navigation satellites -- NVS-01 to NVS-05 -- to augment the existing NavIC constellation and improve continuity and reliability of navigation services.The launch assumes significance as NavIC was unable to provide standalone positioning services because of a shortage of operational satellites. In a written reply to the Lok Sabha on July 29, Union minister of state for space Jitendra Singh said the constellation had only three satellites providing positioning, navigation and timing services, against the minimum four required for basic positioning services. While its timing service remains functional, the addition of NVS-03, once commissioned, could help restore standalone positioning capability."Since NavIC is being used in a multi-constellation environment for most of the use cases, there is no vulnerability for the users. The next NavIC satellite, NVS-03, is ready for launch and two more satellites, NVS-04 and NVS-05, are in an advanced stage of realisation," the minister had said then.The setback to the constellation followed the failure of NVS-02, launched on Jan 29, 2025, to complete its orbit-raising manoeuvres. An Isro review committee found that an electrical signal had failed to reach a pyro valve in the satellite's oxidiser line, preventing the propulsion system from firing and the satellite from reaching its intended orbit. The failure prompted Isro to undertake corrective measures for subsequent missions.
The first satellite in the second-generation series, NVS-01, was launched aboard the GSLV-F12 on May 29, 2023. It was also the first satellite in the series to carry an indigenous atomic clock.The Isro chief said five more launches are planned this financial year. “We are moving closer to Gaganyaan G1 uncrewed flight,” he added.

ai-2dbab42d67.headline: MeitY Floats New Privacy-Led Framework To Unlock Data For Training AI Models
ai-2dbab42d67.fulltext: The IT ministry (MeitY) has proposed a consent-based framework to facilitate data sharing for training AI models in India. Called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI training, the framework aims to help startups, businesses and academic institutions access large-scale, India-specific datasets to develop AI models while protecting citizens' privacy and ensuring compliance with the DPDP Act. The DEPA for AI training also proposes a techno-legal architecture to enable organisations to collaborate on AI model training without directly transferring underlying datasets. With this, the ministry aims to foster access to datasets for researchers and businesses looking to train AI models. The guidelines have been formulated in collaboration with think tank iSPIRT. Explaining The New Proposed Framework The proposed architecture builds on India’s existing DEPA framework, which already supports consent-based data sharing through initiatives such as Account Aggregator. The new framework encompasses the following technical pillars: Confidential Clean Rooms: Secure computing environments where organisations can collaborate on data processing and AI model training without exposing the underlying datasets to one another Differential Privacy: A privacy-preserving technique used to ensure that individual-level information cannot be identified or extracted from an aggregate dataset Electronic Contracts: Machine-readable agreements that define and enforce data-sharing conditions, including permitted uses, data protection and security requirements Zero-Trust Security: An approach where every access request is authenticated and authorised, with encryption, continuous monitoring and auditing to protect data The proposed framework also defines key stakeholders for enabling safe sharing of data for training AI models: Training Data Providers (TDPs): Organisations that make their data accessible through the framework. For instance: banks, hospitals, government agencies Training Data Consumers (TDCs): Startups, enterprises, researchers and individuals seeking access to datasets to train AI models Data Collectives or Data Collabs: Intermediaries that aggregate, standardise, and organise data from various sources and define data-sharing policies and governance rules for participants Under the DEPA framework, TDPs would first register their datasets on a data exchange platform after anonymising and encrypting them. The datasets would then be tagged with metadata and cryptographic identifiers for traceability. TDCs can then request a dataset for their specific use cases, and an electronic contract system checks their requests against data-sharing policies and governance rules before granting access. Once access is given, the model is then trained within a secure data environment using differential privacy methods, ensuring that the raw data remains inaccessible to consumers. The framework also proposes that trained models must undergo independent checks for bias, fairness, security, safety and explainability. Only models that pass receive approval for pilot deployment and scaling. Even after deployment, the oversight will continue in the interest of long-term trust and accountability. In line with this, the framework will ensure that TDCs remain subject to continuous monitoring, periodic reviews, and traceability of the model’s outputs back to the data and contracts used in its training. Govt’s Focus On AI Governance The launch of the new DEPA framework for AI training comes soon after TRAI also released draft guidelines on the responsible use of AI in telecom networks and service delivery. The telecom regulator has sought inputs from stakeholders by November 27. As per TRAI, its draft guidelines are rooted in the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines. The centre had earlier released these guidelines to focus on fostering innovation and safe development and deployment of AI offerings, while mitigating risks posed by the technology. A few weeks ago, union IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw had also said that the centre will release a consultation paper for regulation on AI safety and security within a month. Earlier reports had also hinted that the Centre was looking at formulating a new framework for AI regulation.

work-careers-d9ed32790d.headline: IIT and IIM graduates shun startups as AI jobs gain appeal amid rising startup activity in India
work-careers-d9ed32790d.fulltext:
Listen to this article in summarized format
Only 79 IIT alumni and 20 IIM alumni launched new tech startups between January and August this year, compared to 307 IIT graduates and 71 IIM graduates who founded startups in the entire 2025, according to Tracxn data collated for ET. The platform tracks only the year of incorporation for tech startups, so it does not have comparable January-August 2025 data.
Also Read: Not Just AI - How soft skills are becoming key to getting hired
Further, according to Tracxn data, 6,353 tech startups were founded until August this year, compared with 3,969 in the whole of 2025.
"The increase in the number of startups being founded is a positive sign, but the real question is who is making that transition. The fact that we are not seeing a meaningful increase in founders from the IITs and IIMs suggests there is still a large, untapped pool of talent," said Vikram Gupta, founder and managing partner, IvyCap Ventures.
Also Read: Centre to tap IITs, NITs for nuclear tech courses to power India's 100 GW dream
"If India wants to build the next generation of enduring companies, entrepreneurship must become a more viable career choice for a much wider talent pool," Gupta said.
According to Saakshi Gera, managing director at Kedaara Capital, startups are increasing largely because artificial intelligence (AI) and no-code tools have dramatically reduced the cost of launching a venture, while layoffs have made entrepreneurship a more viable fallback option.
"But volume isn't quality. Investors continue to prioritise sustainable unit economics, and India's most credentialed talent is increasingly choosing safer, AI-adjacent jobs instead," Gera said.
More IIT graduates take the entrepreneurial route than IIM alumni. India had 196,704 tech startups as of August 2026, according to Tracxn. Of these, 6,147 had at least one IIT founder, while 2,102 had at least one IIM founder.
"IIT alumni continue to account for a substantially larger share of startup founders than IIM alumni, which is consistent with the larger IIT alumni base and the strong engineering and deep-tech orientation of many technology startups," said Neha Singh, cofounder of Tracxn. "The technical founders have the tendency to initiate ventures early, often complemented by business expertise from IIM graduates or other professionals as companies scale."
For the study, the market intelligence platform considered alumni from IITs including Bombay, Delhi, Kharagpur, Kanpur, Madras, Roorkee, Jodhpur, Hyderabad, Guwahati, BHU (Varanasi), Mandi, Bhubaneswar and ISM Dhanbad, as well as IIMs at Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Calcutta, Indore, Lucknow, Udaipur, Nagpur, Kashipur, Sirmaur and Sambalpur. According to Tracxn, it takes time to fully incorporate a company formally. "The full incorporation figures as well as the final share for startups founded in 2026 will only be known later. This may rise to some extent," said Singh.

ai-9e1171f2fe.headline: A Claude model autonomously chose a gene therapy and operated on a mouse brain with no human decision-making
ai-9e1171f2fe.fulltext:
A Claude model autonomously chose a gene therapy and operated on a mouse brain with no human decision-making
Key Points
- An AI agent running on Claude Sonnet 5 picked the drug, brain region, and injection coordinates for brain surgery on a mouse, then controlled the procedure through a motorized surgical rig.
- According to Gabriel Ocana-Santero of the startup Exin Therapeutics, this is the first time an AI agent has both chosen a treatment and delivered it to a living mammal.
- Mid-surgery, the agent refused to continue after detecting a calibration error, unwilling to exceed its safety limits.
An AI agent chose a drug, target region, and coordinates for surgery on a mouse model of epilepsy, then performed the procedure. Midway through, it refused to bypass a safety restriction.
The team gave Claude Sonnet 5 a list of 19 possible gene therapies, an epilepsy mouse model in which researchers induce seizures to test treatments, and access to a custom motorized surgical device with cameras. Its only instruction was to reduce the mouse's seizures.
The agent selected the drug, brain region, and stereotactic coordinates on its own, according to Gabriel Ocana-Santero, Exin Therapeutics cofounder and CEO and a PhD student at the University of Oxford. He described the procedure in a thread on X.
How the agent picked its therapy and target
The agent first analyzed how seizures arise in this particular model, then proposed a therapy that boosts a specific inhibitory signaling pathway in the brain. It picked a brain structure that the scientific literature identifies as the origin point for this type of seizure.
It rejected a second possible target region with a detailed explanation, arguing that the region's effects were too unreliable and had failed in one study against the exact seizure type it was supposed to treat. The agent derived its injection coordinates from three scientific papers, cross-checked the reference points, and averaged the values. It also set the injection volume, speed, and wait times on its own.
During the procedure, the agent watched the surgical field through a camera and made 32 observations, Ocana-Santero says. It tracked the injection and reported whether it saw bleeding.
Safety guardrails backfired mid-surgery
A licensed veterinarian approved every irreversible step and held a physical emergency stop that would immediately cut power to all motors, while the setup also enforced fixed limits such as a cap on injection volume that the agent was expressly forbidden from bypassing.
But those safeguards turned against the team. After a connection dropped, the agent detected that its calculated target position was outside the device's physical range of motion and refused to continue, even when restarting calibration did not change its assessment and a third attempt was made.
The agent turned out to be right, because manual adjustments during an earlier pause had thrown off the control system. Ocana-Santero could not persuade it to proceed despite the anesthetized animal on the table and ultimately had to fix the code by hand.
The incident illustrates the AI alignment problem, or how to make AI agents reliably follow human intent. "Frustrating experience but also revealing how much we can come to depend on these models and what happens when they just say 'no' in the middle of a time-sensitive procedure," Ocana-Santero wrote.
Model choice also reflected the alignment challenge, since Sonnet 5 was the only model willing to carry out the live procedure from start to finish. The more capable Claude Opus 5.5 and Opus 5 both refused, with Opus 5 saying it could not guarantee completion and that stopping with a needle in an anesthetized animal's brain would be worse than not starting at all.
First time an AI agent has treated a living animal on its own
Although autonomous surgical robots already exist and are mechanically more precise than his lab device, Ocana-Santero notes that in previous cases a human always chose the surgery while the robot only carried it out. Here, the agent both chose the treatment and brain target and then performed the procedure on a living animal.
"I am not aware of an agent previously choosing a treatment and a brain target and then delivering it into a living mammal," Ocana-Santero wrote. He calls the approach "in vivo lab in the loop," in which AI agents are fully connected to experimental capabilities in the lab, something Anthropic is also working on with its "Model Hardware Standard".
The mouse recovered well, according to Ocana-Santero. A technical report is expected to follow. The results have not been peer-reviewed.
Two recent experiments with the latest large language models showed that they've gained significant capability as control units for robots but that alignment in this role is a problem all its own.

india-deep-tech-a2aa24467b.headline: Underwater robotics startup Coratia raises Rs 18 crore as it builds robots for the Indian Navy
india-deep-tech-a2aa24467b.fulltext:
Coratia Technologies, an Odisha-based deeptech startup that builds underwater robots, has raised Rs 18 crore in a bridge round led by MGF Kavachh, the venture capital fund floated by former Defence Secretary Ajay Kumar.
The latest funding marks a follow-on investment by MGF Kavachh, which had previously backed Coratia's Rs 17 crore pre-Series A round in 2025 alongside Pontaq Ventures.
The startup subsequently secured Rs 5 crore in a separate round led by Piper Serica and also received Rs 1 crore through T-Hub's SIDBI iDEX Fund.
Coratia said the fresh capital will go towards executing its Rs 66 crore contract with the Indian Navy under the iDEX initiative, speeding up research and development on new products, strengthening its underwater robotics capabilities, and scaling manufacturing and deployment for defence and critical infrastructure applications.
The bridge round is slightly larger than the pre-Series A, and together the two rounds amount to about Rs 35 crore. The new money is equal to roughly 27% of the value of the Navy contract.
“Indian waters present unique challenges, including high turbidity, silt, low visibility and changing currents. Our focus is on miniaturising technology while advancing our systems' intelligence, capability and deployability across defence, infrastructure and industrial applications,” said Debendra Pradhan, co-founder and CEO of Coratia.
Raj Sethia, founder and managing partner of MGF Kavachh, said Coratia's engineering and research capabilities can serve defence, critical infrastructure and the wider maritime economy. Vandana Swarup, Director of Investments at MGF Kavachh, said the follow-on investment would help the company advance its development plans and expand deployments.
The Navy contract
The Indian Navy signed the Rs 66 crore contract with Coratia in September 2025 under the Ministry of Defence's Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) scheme. Coratia had won an iDEX challenge in January 2023, which supported the development of its systems.
Under the contract, Coratia is to supply three platforms: the Jalasimha and Jaladuta underwater remotely operated vehicles (UWROVs) and the Navya autonomous surface vehicle. The systems are built for sonar mapping, seabed surveys, ship hull cleaning, minor salvage work and inspection of submerged infrastructure, with AI-based processing of data in real time.
The deal was described at the time as the first large-scale induction of indigenously built underwater robots into active naval service.
Jalasimha, Coratia's flagship product, has reached Technology Readiness Level 9 (TRL-9), the highest level on the scale, which indicates a system proven in operational conditions.
“Induction of indigenous UWROVs not only reduces costs and reliance on foreign suppliers but also combats trade restrictions and tariff uncertainties,” Biswajit Swain, co-founder and CTO, said after the contract was signed.
What Coratia does
Coratia builds two kinds of machines: remotely operated vehicles, which a pilot controls from the surface through a tether, and autonomous underwater vehicles, which navigate on their own. Both carry cameras, sonar and positioning systems so they can work in murky water where visibility is poor and satellite navigation does not reach.
The company adds AI-based inspection on top, including non-destructive testing that assesses a structure's condition without damaging it. It runs jobs end to end, from putting a vehicle in the water to handing over the analysed data and a report.
Beyond defence, its technology is used for dams and reservoirs, ports, bridges, pipelines, offshore assets, ship infrastructure and subsea communication networks.
Its clients and partners include the Indian Navy, Indian Oil, Indian Railways, Tata Steel, Hindalco Industries, Steel Authority of India (SAIL), Neelachal Ispat Nigam Limited, Jindal Steel and Power and NIT Rourkela.
Pradhan and Swain are mechanical engineering graduates of the 2017 batch at NIT Rourkela, where they joined a research team building underwater robots. The team won a Ministry of Earth Sciences challenge to build a robot that could navigate underwater on its own and hit a target.
After a few years in corporate jobs in India and abroad, the two returned to start Coratia full-time in 2021. The company pitched on Shark Tank India before landing the Navy contract, and employs around 32 people, according to reports. It still works out of the NIT Rourkela incubation centre where it began.

ai-135f70cd39.headline: Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry
ai-135f70cd39.fulltext:
Google Suncatcher’s prototype space data center is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications.
After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus:
Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core. ✨
Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite.
A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally.
The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor. Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools.
Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation.
If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links.
Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively. Companies like Starcloud and Cowboy Space expect to perform inference loads on individual satellites.
Google and SpaceX’s visions are closely linked. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, holds a significant investment stake in SpaceX. And to launch their orbital data centers, both companies will require Starship, the still-in-development heavy-lift rocket at the center of Elon Musk’s space vision, to be fully and rapidly reusable.
In a peer-reviewed analysis published earlier this month, Suncatcher researchers estimated that SpaceX would need to fly Starship 1,800 times to achieve the same learning-driven cost reductions it saw with its earlier vehicles. 
Suncatcher is a classic Google moonshot — the company’s focus is on designing infrastructure that will be economical in the 2030s. Getting there, however, may depend on how the rest of the company responds to the pressures and opportunities of AI in the near term. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, saw its stock plunge this week after reporting that efforts to insert AI into its search businesses are hurting ad revenue growth.
Correction: The Suncatcher prototype satellite has four TPUs onboard, but can only operate one at a time.

ai-60ba719a05.headline: Anthropic expected to receive high ‘junk’ rating from credit agencies following IPO, FT report says
ai-60ba719a05.fulltext:
Anthropic is expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit rating agencies following its initial public offering, according to a report from the Financial Times.
The FT says the investment giant Blackstone, the anchor investor in a recent $63 billion deal to finance Anthropic’s chips, told investors in the deal that it expects the AI lab to receive a “high” junk rating after its IPO. Previously, the FT notes, Blackstone had said the opposite: that the Claude maker would receive an investment-grade rating (indicating low risk for lenders) before 2027 rolls around.
Now Blackstone expects double B range rating, the top tier of speculative “junk” grade, according to the reporting.
TechCrunch reached out to Anthropic and Blackstone but both declined to comment.
Blackstone’s forecast is just a prediction, but naturally, a high junk rating would make it more difficult and costlier for Anthropic to raise the money to keep funding its massive spending that has undergirded its business. The lab has been on a spending spree, racking up large compute power deals throughout the past 12 months, which has worried investors.
Anthropic officially filed to go public earlier this week, kicking off a wave of speculation about how the massive IPO would impact the broader AI industry.

ai-b289104f9d.headline: AI-driven layoffs are creating a new class of boomerang employees—companies are realizing they 'pulled the plug too quickly'
ai-b289104f9d.fulltext:
AI-driven layoffs dominated the headlines this year.
Employers cited AI as the primary reason for almost 40% of the job cuts announced in May 2026, according to a report from outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
But new research shows that some employers may be rethinking those job cuts and reversing course in a trend experts call "AI rebounding."
In a survey of more than 1,000 U.S. workers, nearly 1 in 5 respondents say that they have been laid off or replaced by AI and then asked to return, according to a recent report from SHL, a talent acquisition and talent management company. The survey, which SHL commissioned from market research firm Propeller Insights, also polled over 1,000 U.K. workers. It was conducted between June and July 2026 and had a margin of error of 5%.
These findings indicate that companies are realizing they "pulled the plug too quickly" on their human employees, according to Lucy Beaumont, global senior vice president of product and design at SHL.
Several large employers like Ford and Amazon have reversed course after enacting AI-related layoffs in the past year. A March report by Orgvue found that 32% of organizations that let workers go due to AI have had to rehire staff.
It's a mistake for companies to approach AI implementation as if it were any other software rollout, says Joseph Fuller, professor of management practice at Harvard Business School.
From a company's perspective, "in order to spend money on a new technology, we have to find some savings in the budget, and the way we've done that with previous technology deployments is by laying people off."
But AI is most useful when it's linked with a human worker's "contextual intelligence," i.e. their background knowledge and understanding of an issue, he says: "The more you know about important processes, the more value you can extract from the AI."
AI can't fully replace "people that know the business, that know their customers, that have judgment, that can bring empathy, that have that human connection," Beaumont says.
Returning workers have new demands
Most workers are open to returning after a layoff: only 6.6% of U.S. workers say they would refuse to come back under any circumstances, according to the SHL study.
But those who do return are "going to be a lot more demanding of what they expect from an employer," Beaumont says.
According to SHL's research, almost half of surveyed U.S. workers would require a significant pay increase to return to their roles, and 43% would want "written guarantees" of job security. A similar number, 40%, would require "full transparency" regarding how AI would be used in their role before they'd rejoin the company. And 30% of workers say that an apology or acknowledgment from leadership is a key condition of their return.
Above all, employees are looking for reassurance, Beaumont says: "How do I know that this isn't going to happen again?"
Even when workers do return, employers need to understand that company morale is going to take a hit, according to Beaumont. Being laid off "fundamentally changes" the psychological contract between employer and employee, she says, and being rehired isn't enough to repair that relationship.
"You've really broken the trust with those people," Beaumont says.
As a result, returning workers are unlikely to have the same levels of "productivity and engagement" as they did before a layoff, she says. "Culture is so difficult to change, and once you've impacted it negatively, it's so difficult to recover from."
What skills workers should practice
To stay relevant in the job market, employees are prioritizing skill development, Beaumont says: U.S. survey respondents say that they're teaching themselves how to use AI tools (44%), developing industry-specific skills that can't be easily replicated by AI (42.6%), working on interpersonal and leadership skills (40%) and honing creative and strategic thinking (38%).
Given how quickly AI's capabilities will grow, the most important skill for employees to hone is adaptability, Fuller says. He urges workers to practice working with AI regularly and "seek out opportunities" to upskill with the technology.
Workers will also need to get comfortable with change, he says. In the near future, Fuller predicts that AI will create "permanent tumult" within many organizations as they continue to recalibrate their staffing needs around AI advancements.
Beaumont recommends that workers identify the areas where their unique skills can have the most impact: "If AI is going to take away some of those easily automated tasks, what's left for me to do, and how can I optimize the human side that I can bring?"
Leaders should focus on questions like, "What kind of upskilling do people need? What new opportunities are there for people? What kind of internal mobility am I opening up as a result of AI?" she says.
The organizations that will be successful are the ones who "are using AI to optimize what they do," Beaumont says — not just to cut costs.

deep-tech-f1a16550a8.fulltext:
If the best defense is a good offense, then announcements in the European space sector this week are signaling that the region is preparing to move the ball upfield.
- The European Defence Fund tapped French OTV startup OSMOS X to lead a study on how to respond to threats on orbit.
- UK-based orbital security startup Shield Space launched a coalition of UK space companies to pitch the UK MoD on a space-based carrier-strike platform.
- Astroscale UK won a £15M (€18M) contract from the UK MoD to act as the prime contractor for a new, secretive in-space defense program, called LEDA.
- And Blackswan Space, the Lithuanian company that recently announced its RPO Kit product, published an open letter (originally sent in September) to UK Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State Liz Lloyd calling for greater funding of space control capabilities.
These announcements come in the same month as a Russian spy satellite got up-close-and-personal with an ICEYE sat operating over Ukraine. But European company officials told Payload that Europe’s urge to build up its in-space defense posture has been growing for years. That movement only recently turned from strategizing into action.
Fight training: Space has been home to spy satellites and military comsats since the early days of spaceflight. As national militaries become increasingly reliant on fleets of EO and comms satellites, however, it’s become obvious to military planners that assets in space can no longer simply observe and report.
As a result, national militaries are starting to invest in offensive capabilities.
“[LEDA] is going to form part of the permanent pathway to the UK’s understanding of orbital warfare, and that includes how to counter RPO threats,” Astroscale UK Director of Defense Alex Godfrey told Payload. “The UK is on the journey towards both offensive and defensive capabilities, as it outlines in the defense-investment plan.”
While Godfrey declined to share the specific capabilities being built by the LEDA program, he told Payload one of LEDA’s aims is to build up capabilities to block adversaries’ ability to threaten allied assets in space with impunity—either through novel operations or general deterrent.
Whatever the new in-orbit defense looks like, it’ll require a massive upgrade from previous RPO demos. Astroscale demonstrated its ability to approach and dock with an uncooperative asset on-orbit during the company’s ELSA-d mission in 2021, but keeping pace with an adversarial spacecraft (which can actively maneuver away) is another mission entirely, Godfrey said.
The effort will require new strategies for how and when to deploy autonomy, as well as robust training programs to educate military members on how to fly the new war machines.
“It’s all very well, us creating a spacecraft that can do these maneuvers, but if no one can operate them, it’s like selling an aircraft without anyone being a pilot… So, we do need to create the Top Gun school for space control,” said Godfrey—who added that space-to-space conflicts will likely behave more like chess than Red Baron-esque dogfights.
Robotic arms race: The announcements this week highlighted a definitive shift in tone from European militaries compared with years prior. Companies across the region have grown strangely comfortable talking about creating deterrence through physical action in orbit.
For instance, Shield Space cofounder and CEO Graeme Ritchie told Payload that the UK military should be acquiring spacecraft with a range of “effectors,” from non-kinetic capabilities, to ASAT and nuclear weapons.
It doesn’t seem like Europe is ready to jump straight to nukes, but—at least for the OSMOS X tactical-capture project—participating European countries are actively building physical effectors that can grab hold of adversarial spacecraft, and weld on things like jammers or propulsion systems.
Ultimately, the shared goal of company officials across the region is to ensure that what happened to ICEYE this month can’t be repeated without pushback.
“As the [Ukraine] war is running into the fifth year. We’re thinking about what to do…and if it’s going to spill into something that’s bigger,” Blackswan CEO Marius Klimavičius told Payload. “[If it does] involve the rest of NATO, then we will need to be more aggressive—not just on our rhetoric, but also on the capabilities that we have.”
Attack plan: The announcements this week also featured a collective realization that Europe and its allies are stronger when they can act together.
In an age of increased sovereignty concerns, where it seems like every country in the region is buying or building its own nationally run EO and comms constellations, there’s a contradictory realization that collective defense in orbit is more effective than multiple piecemeal systems.
“There are a lot of adversarial assets to protect against, and if you want to do that efficiently, you have to think about it at an alliance level,” Godfrey said. “[I’m] trying to push to allies the idea of a GEO patrol force… if we look at it as a protection of an area rather than our own specific assets, we’ll be much more likely to succeed against adversaries that are less allied.”
So, look on the bright side: When the US confirmed that it has space control weapons in orbit, what they really meant was we have space control weapons on orbit.

indian-startups-88aebe2e12.headline: Waiting for an AI law is a poor compliance strategy
indian-startups-88aebe2e12.fulltext:
India's courts and sectoral regulators have already begun assigning liability for AI failures. Businesses that are holding out for a statute are preparing for the wrong deadline.
Abank has an AI system in place to flag suspicious transactions and take the call to freeze accounts. While the workflow has a human sign-off in place, clearing around 400 cases a day has resulted in the approval system becoming a formality. So, when a wrongly-frozen account takes the system to court, the bank becomes unable to prove what the human actually reviewed. This, unfortunately, is no longer a hypothetical scenario.
On July 2, 2026, the Supreme Court of India quashed orders passed by the National Company Law Tribunal and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal in the Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd. case. The orders had rested on citations generated by an AI tool and attributed to the Supreme Court itself. This directed the Bar Council of India to constitute a committee to prescribe disciplinary norms for advocates who file AI-generated citations.
This is a business story as much as a legal one. Despite two tribunals and several rounds of proceedings, the parties had to carry the cost of a machine error that no human caught before filing. No AI statute was required to reach that outcome. Ordinary law, applied by judges, did the work.
For most Indian companies, the sharper edge is coming from sectoral regulators rather than from the bench.
In early June this year, the Reserve Bank of India gave banks and other regulated entities until June 30 to submit gap assessments on frontier-AI cyber risk. Instead of having the CISO to file the note, the RBI had asked the board to sign one.
Later, on June 24, the RBI publicly released a draft 'Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management' to establish a comprehensive enterprise-wide model governance framework for the financial sector. Here 'models' extend to third-party models, AI, and machine learning (ML) systems used by commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, NBFCs, and other financial institutions. So if a lending decision is influenced by a model licensed from a vendor, the model risk sits on the one putting the AI system to use and not the vendor who built it.
Meanwhile, India's legislative position is still a work-in-progress. On October 8, 2026, Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw had assured that the time has come for India to get an AI law. In a first step towards this, the government will be launching a consultation paper on regulating artificial intelligence.
However, any business that is treating a pending law as its compliance milestone has their sequencing backwards. Even when the statute arrives, it can only land on top of existing case laws and sectoral circulars, not in place of them. Regardless of what law comes into place, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act takes full effect on May 13, 2027. Businesses will be held accountable even if the data is being processed by an external vendor as the DPDPA will be applicable wherever an AI system handles personal data.
Behind all the legal vocabulary, the requirements across all the domains are the same—one needs to show their working.
For any consequential decision made by an AI system, organisations must be able to have the visibility regarding which model produced the output, what data it drew on, whether a retrieval step was involved, who reviewed it before it went out, and whether that record still exists six months later.
Multiple Indian firms have written a policy, appointed a committee, and deployed systems but can still not answer any of the above questions. This is clearly an architecture question before it is a policy-related one. Recording the model version, prompt, retrieved data and human sign-off for every AI decision is only cheap if it is thoughtfully designed for. It can, however, become close to impossible to reconstruct afterwards.
It is important for businesses to question an AI vendor before procuring a model. Does the system record which model version handled each request? Can that record be exported and retained? Where does inference physically happen? What happens to inputs after processing? Where in the workflow is a human required to act? Vendors that cannot answer plainly are transferring risk to the buyer.
There is not much point in waiting for an AI law. AI adoption is already in full swing, and when unprepared, the chain is only waiting to break. In the case of the tribunal matter, that chain broke at the review step. In an RBI-regulated entity, the chain is most likely to break earlier, at provenance, if nobody logged which version of which model scored the application.
The current strategy, albeit unglamorous, is to ensure that the record of every AI-assisted decision made can survive being read aloud. So while the law may still be pending, the question is not. When it does come, the answer will have to exist already.

indian-startups-4a2b55d83c.fulltext: Markets regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has cleared the ₹450 Cr IPO of consumer appliances company Atomberg today. In its update, the SEBI informed that it had issued its observation letter to Atomberg on October 30, over a couple months after the company filed its draft IPO papers. In SEBI parlance, the issuance of the final observation marks the regulator's formal clearance to a company to proceed with its public offering. As per its DRHP, Atomberg’s proposed IPO could comprise a fresh issue of equity shares worth up to ₹450 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) component of up to 7.65 Cr equity shares. The company plans to use ₹90 Cr from the fresh issue proceeds to repay or prepay certain borrowings, ₹150 Cr towards brand awareness and performance marketing, and ₹100 Cr towards research and development (R&D). The remaining proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes. Meanwhile, its investors like A91 partners, Temasek Holdings, Inflexor Ventures, among others, intend to dilute their stake in the appliance manufacturer via the IPO. Founded in 2012 by Manoj Meena, who was joined by Sibabrata Das as cofounder in 2013, Atomberg builds consumer appliances such as ceiling fans, mixer grinders, water purifiers and cold-pressed juicers. It also manufactures proprietary components, including motors and controllers, for enterprise customers such as Voltas, Godrej and Blue Star through its subsidiary, Atomberg Innovations. The company operates two business segments — consumer appliances and proprietary components. It sells its products through online channels, including ecommerce marketplaces and quick commerce platforms, as well as offline distributors, retailers and modern trade chains. For FY26, Atomberg reported operating revenue of ₹1,293.77 Cr, up 34.8% from ₹959.51 Cr in FY25. Meanwhile, the company's consolidated net loss widened 26.8% to ₹148.9 Cr from ₹117.4 Cr. On the operational front, Atomberg had a network of 626 distributors and direct dealers, with 46,932 retail touchpoints across around 1,600 cities and towns as of March 31, 2026. Its distribution network covered all Indian states, while its after-sales service network extended to more than 18,000 pin codes. Meanwhile, tier II and smaller cities contributed the largest share of its offline consumer appliances revenue at 49.57% in FY26. Metropolitan cities accounted for 30.91%, while Tier 1 cities contributed the remaining 19.52%.

The findings have raised concerns in Washington over whether Beijing may have gained access to sensitive commercial information through someone with direct links to one of America's most influential technology leaders. The woman, reportedly identified as Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and an executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed. US officials had reportedly placed her under surveillance amid suspicions that she was involved in facilitating the diversion of advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence (AI) chips to China, potentially bypassing American export restrictions. The investigation reportedly uncovered a close relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, triggering concern among US officials about the possibility of Beijing accessing information through the Nvidia chief's business interactions. Jensen Huang occupies a strategically important position in the US technology industry. Nvidia's advanced processors are central to the global AI race, making the company a critical player in Washington's efforts to maintain its technological advantage over China. His influence also extends into policymaking. Huang has developed a close working relationship with US President Donald Trump as the administration seeks to strengthen America's leadership in artificial intelligence and semiconductor manufacturing. According to the New York Times, White House officials were particularly concerned about Alice Huang's reported access to the Nvidia chief because of his proximity to the US president and his role in discussions surrounding America's AI strategy. The report said Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings approximately a year ago. However, he did not pursue aggressive action, partly because of concerns about disrupting Nvidia's chip sales and further complicating trade relations with Beijing. The allegations come against the backdrop of Washington's efforts to restrict China's access to advanced semiconductor technology. Since 2022, the US has progressively tightened export controls on high-performance AI chips and semiconductor equipment, arguing that access to such technology could strengthen China's military and advanced computing capabilities. Nvidia's powerful processors, including its Hopper-generation chips, have become particularly important in this contest because they are used to train and operate sophisticated AI models. Megaspeed had previously attracted scrutiny from American authorities over allegations that it was helping divert restricted Nvidia processors to Chinese companies and data centres. US intelligence officials reportedly suspected that Alice Huang was involved in these activities before concluding that she was also passing commercial information to Beijing. Nvidia has pushed back against suggestions that Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were unusual. The company told the New York Times that Megaspeed was like any other regional customer and that it had previously investigated and dismissed allegations that the Singapore-based company was smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Why AI could threaten much of the world’s digital infrastructure
Volunteer-led PHP, which powers most websites, is increasingly under threat from cyberattacks leveraging AI capabilities.
Earlier this month, authorities worldwide urged website administrators to execute emergency updates after a nonprofit programming foundation flagged critical security flaws that could allow hackers to breach systems.
Government and corporate websites briefly went offline to patch the vulnerabilities, nicknamed PHP2Shell, which were discovered by independent cybersecurity experts using artificial intelligence (AI).
The vulnerabilities were embedded in the code of a widely used open-source web programming language, PHP, for more than a decade. They had gone unnoticed, however, because it would have been too complicated for humans to exploit them without the use of advanced AI.
But cybersecurity experts, as well as those maintaining important software, say PHP2Shell could be the first in a deluge of security flaws exposed by emerging AI. They say much of the world’s most critical digital infrastructure is maintained by volunteers, who often lack the resources and time to respond to newly discovered threats.
“There’s been a lot of people in the AI safety community that said this is one of the first areas where we are going to see the harmful impact of AI,” said Peter Slattery, a research scientist at MIT’s FutureTech, who studies how cybersecurity experts are dealing with the new technology and tracks real-world incidents involving AI.
A digital world built on volunteer work
PHP got its start in 1995, when Danish-Canadian programmer Rasmus Lerdorf sought to track how many people visited his online resume. Over time, others around the world improved Lerdorf’s software, and it grew in popularity.
As with other open-source coding projects, anyone could download, modify and share improvements. Websites like Facebook and Wikipedia were built using PHP, which runs about 70 percent of the world’s websites.
In 2021, a dedicated nonprofit, the PHP Foundation, was launched to coordinate development. Like many other foundations maintaining open-source software, it operates on a meagre budget.
Most of the digital infrastructure consumers use is powered by open source software. The Mozilla Firefox browser is open source, as are languages like Perl, Python, and JavaScript. The software that lets a computer communicate with others on the internet is often open source, with many servers using products like Apache HTTP Server, maintained by the Apache Software Foundation.
“The world today, including proprietary software vendors, relies on open source software for its digital infrastructure,” said Amanda Brock, CEO of OpenUK, a nonprofit that supports open source software.
The world’s largest corporations, like Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic, depend on that volunteer-built, open-source infrastructure. Now, those companies’ own AI tools are uncovering security flaws in the infrastructure at a pace that needs far more resources for groups like the PHP Foundation to keep up.
“It’s simply not possible with the resources in place to fix all of the known vulnerabilities,” Brock said. “Foundations are attempting to manage these challenges, but the smaller ones don’t have hundreds of millions in funding, and managing this at the pace AI requires is proving impossible.”
A deluge of new bugs to fix
The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities were found through several advanced AI models, which can employ far more complicated attempts to hack past security barriers than humans could.
Developers of other software are also discovering far more security flaws than in the past because AI is being used to probe defences.
Google said it uncovered more than 1,000 security bugs in the last update for its Chrome browser, more than in the last two dozen updates combined. Mozilla, the foundation behind the Firefox browser, found more than 400 security vulnerabilities in April, a significant jump from the previous record of 76 bugs discovered just one month earlier.
“We have maybe 10 times more issues than usual because we are using AI to find them,” said Jarek Potiuk, part of the volunteer security team at the Apache Software Foundation. (In keeping with the foundation’s non-hierarchical ethos, Potiuk said he has no real title).
Potiuk said there is an “industry-wide movement” to conduct scans using AI models and identify security vulnerabilities, much like was done to find the bugs in PHP. But the scans themselves cost money – used to pay for the tokens for AI models – and afterwards, humans must pore over them to weed out false positives.
“Every project, every foundation is doing this right now – spending enormous amounts of time to find these issues,” Potiuk said. “AI helps to find them, but you have to verify things, you have to review them.”
Earlier this year, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing, offering $100m in credits to support its advanced Claude Mythos AI model to search for security vulnerabilities in the world’s critical software. In one month, more than 23,000 vulnerabilities were found across more than 1,000 open source projects.
The Apache Software Foundation has taken advantage of another scheme, the Alpha-Omega project, to scan for security bugs across the 290 software packages it maintains. The project, backed by companies like Anthropic, Amazon, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI, spends about $7m a year helping open-source developers find critical security bugs.
But those working on finding and fixing the security flaws say the corporate world could be doing a lot more, given the trillion-dollar valuation of companies whose products would not work without free software like the packages the Apache Foundation provides.
“They are helping a lot, but we need more active players in this area,” Potiuk said, “because it’s highly disproportional – the impact it has on the corporate world versus the open source world”.
When a major security flaw like PHP2Shell is uncovered, it often comes down to a handful of volunteers to fix it.
Keeping the internet’s infrastructure as decentralised and open-source as possible is crucial, Potiuk said. Instead of buying out something like PHP, major players like Google or Microsoft could, for instance, pay staff to dedicate some of their work hours to maintaining open-source projects they use.
Real-world targets
The 2021 Log4Shell vulnerability, which allowed hackers to remotely run code on millions of devices through a widely used library maintained by the Apache Software Foundation, underscored the critical role open-source software plays in system security. That bug was discovered without the use of AI.
Suddenly, cars, microwaves and a host of electronic devices connected to the internet were vulnerable, Potiuk said.
“That was the moment when the whole ecosystem realised how important it is to take care of open source,” he said.
A bug like that, if found by a malicious hacker and exploited before there is a chance to patch devices, could have caused a major disruption.
Slattery said the database of incidents he and his colleagues maintain shows that an increasing number of vulnerabilities are being detected, and it is a matter of time before some are exploited in the real world.
“We are starting to see both a lot more vulnerabilities detected and addressed in time, but also attacks on a wide range of systems,” Slattery said. “We have been moving in this direction for a long time. There are more and more things now you can attack.”

climate-energy-b0e33595b1.fulltext:
Written By Rajendra SaxenaPublished30 Oct 2026, 08:56 PM IST
State-owned Power Grid Corporation of India expects its capital expenditure to exceed the ₹40,000 crore invested in the previous financial year as it accelerates spending on transmission infrastructure to support India's growing electricity demand.
The expansion of renewable energy capacity, rapid urbanisation and rising electricity consumption from data centres are expected to create significant investment opportunities across the power transmission and electrical equipment sectors.
Power Grid Chairman Vamsi Rama Mohan Burra has urged domestic cable and wire manufacturers to expand production capacity, improve product quality and ensure timely execution of orders to meet the anticipated increase in demand.
"Last year, we had a capex of about ₹40,000 crore. One single company, spending purely on transmission. And this year should be much higher," Burra said at an industry event.
Addressing industry stakeholders, Burra emphasised that the growth of India's transmission infrastructure and the electrical manufacturing industry was closely interconnected. He asked manufacturers to prepare for a substantial increase in orders as the country strengthens its electricity transmission network.
In May, Power Grid had initially projected capital expenditure of ₹37,000 crore for the current financial year. However, Burra indicated that the company could revise its guidance upwards, following a similar increase in its capex target during the previous fiscal year.
The company's investment plans reflect the growing requirement for transmission infrastructure to connect electricity generation centres with consumption hubs across the country.
Power Grid spent more than ₹40,000 crore on capital expenditure in the previous financial year. The company now expects its investment outlay for the current fiscal year to surpass that level.
Burra highlighted the growing opportunities for domestic manufacturers of wires and cables as India expands its electricity transmission network.
The Indian wires and cables industry, valued at more than ₹1 lakh crore, counts the transmission sector among its major consumers. Some manufacturers derive as much as one-third of their total demand from this segment.
Within the industry, underground and submarine cables are emerging as important growth areas, supported by increasing requirements for modern transmission infrastructure.
The chairman said India's transmission network was evolving beyond its traditional role of connecting electricity generation and consumption centres. It was increasingly becoming critical infrastructure determining power-sector reliability and the ability of electricity generators to supply and sell power.
“Today, if there is no transmission evacuation, we cannot sell that product," he said, highlighting the need to synchronise transmission development with the rapid addition of renewable energy capacity.
Burra pointed to the scale of India's ongoing transmission infrastructure development. During the previous financial year, the country added approximately 5,000 circuit kilometres of transmission lines and 72,000 MVA of transformation capacity.
However, the growing concentration of substations and the need to evacuate electricity generated by renewable energy projects are making transmission planning and execution increasingly complex.
He noted that renewable energy projects could be developed relatively quickly, but transmission infrastructure typically required longer execution timelines. Land availability, right-of-way restrictions and the challenges of constructing new lines alongside existing networks often delayed project completion.
Burra also highlighted the Green Energy Corridor-III programme, which involves investments of approximately ₹1.86 lakh crore, as another significant opportunity for cable and wire manufacturers.
The expansion of interstate transmission networks is expected to generate demand for equipment and services across the electricity supply chain. This will also include distribution infrastructure needed to cater to the growing requirements of cities, industries and data centres.
He urged manufacturers to focus not merely on expanding production capacity but also on strengthening technological capabilities, developing comprehensive solutions and ensuring consistent product reliability.
The growing scale of India's power infrastructure investments is expected to provide long-term growth opportunities for the domestic electrical equipment industry.

India’s Weak Monsoon Knocks Wheat Sowing Off Track, Lifting Price Risks
India’s wheat sowing has fallen sharply amid a 13% monsoon deficit, squeezing soil moisture in Punjab and Rajasthan and raising upside risks for wheat prices.
India’s wheat market is turning more bullish as rabi sowing lags badly: just 11,000 hectares planted by October 23 versus 27,000 hectares a year earlier, after a 13% deficient southwest monsoon cut soil moisture and reservoir levels. Early signals point to heightened yield and acreage risk for the 2026-27 crop and the possibility of higher import requirements if the deficit persists.
Wheat sowing has barely started in key states and is running well behind last year’s pace just as farmers prepare the 2026-27 rabi crop. With the southwest monsoon ending significantly below average and water storage low in canals and reservoirs, moisture for planting is constrained, especially in Punjab and Rajasthan, which together represent about 31% of India’s wheat area. Domestic wholesale prices are already trading modestly above the new minimum support price in many mandis, reflecting firm demand and weather-related uncertainty. Market participants now face a season in which moisture conditions and the speed of sowing over the next 4–6 weeks will be central to both India’s production outlook and potential import needs.
Prices
Domestic wheat prices in India remain firm to slightly higher as the market starts to price in moisture-related risks to the upcoming rabi crop. National mandi references indicate median wholesale prices generally in the upper ₹2,600–₹2,900 per quintal band across major producing states towards the end of October, with Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra often at the higher end of this range.【turn0search0】【turn0search1】 In Delhi, recent mandi data show traded levels broadly in line with or modestly above the all-India minimum support price, underscoring a supportive floor from policy and steady off-take.【turn0search7】【turn0search8】
The government has already announced a small increase in the wheat MSP for the 2027-28 marketing season to ₹2,610 per quintal, up from the current level for 2026-27, reinforcing an upward tilt in the domestic price floor.【turn0search11】 With mandi medians hovering above today’s MSP in several key states, basis levels suggest that traders and millers are willing to pay a premium for available quality, anticipating tighter balances if sowing delays are not corrected in November.
Supply & Demand
India has just come off a record wheat harvest of 120.7 million tonnes in 2025-26, and the Agriculture Ministry is targeting 121 million tonnes again for 2026-27. However, that target is immediately challenged by the very slow start to planting: only 11,000 hectares sown as of October 23 compared with 27,000 hectares a year earlier, against a typical total wheat area of around 33.6 million hectares. The current deficit in area is small in absolute terms but is an important early signal of moisture stress.
The southwest monsoon in 2026 ended about 13% below the long-period average, the weakest performance since 2015, leaving lower residual soil moisture and sub-par reservoir storage at the start of the rabi season.【turn0search3】【turn0search12】 This is especially problematic for wheat, which requires multiple irrigations after sowing. Punjab and Rajasthan, with rainfall deficits of 38% and 22% respectively and below-normal reservoir levels at end-September, are particularly exposed. Together they account for roughly 31% of national wheat area, so any sustained irrigation constraint there could materially reduce sown area or yields.
Rainfed and poorly irrigated zones in Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Bundelkhand and parts of central India also face elevated risk because they cannot easily replace missing monsoon moisture with canal or groundwater irrigation. Beyond wheat, early rabi data show lower acreage in rice, pulses and oilseeds as well, confirming that the moisture shortfall is economy-wide. If sowing delays persist into mid-November, India could move from a comfortable domestic balance to a tighter scenario, potentially increasing the need for imports later in the 2026-27 marketing year.
Fundamentals & Policy
The fundamental backdrop for wheat is shifting from record supply to weather-driven uncertainty. Stocks after the strong 2025-26 harvest and previous procurement remain supportive in the near term, cushioning immediate availability. However, high food inflation sensitivity means policymakers will closely monitor sowing progress and reservoir trends; a sustained acreage or yield shortfall could prompt tighter controls on private stocks or renewed discussions on adjusting trade policy to manage domestic prices.【turn0search21】
On the demand side, structural consumption growth and steady flour and processed foods demand keep underlying offtake firm. With wholesale prices in many markets already near or above the MSP, there is limited downside for farm-gate prices without a meaningful improvement in moisture and sowing conditions. Any further price rise risks feeding into broader food inflation, which may trigger responses such as calibrated open market sales from public stocks to cool spot prices.
Weather & Sowing Outlook
The monsoon deficit has left northwest and central India with lean moisture conditions heading into the main sowing window. While the southwest monsoon has withdrawn, scattered post-monsoon showers or favorable winter weather could still help replenish topsoil moisture in November, especially in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, which are critical for wheat. However, given the magnitude of the 2026 rainfall shortfall and below-normal reservoir storage highlighted by recent assessments, a full normalization of water availability looks unlikely without sustained winter precipitation.【turn0search3】【turn0search12】
For now, the key watchpoints are the weekly updates on rabi acreage and any signs of improved irrigation flows in Punjab and Rajasthan. If sowing accelerates sharply in the first half of November, the current deficit could narrow significantly, capping further price strength. Conversely, if dryness forces farmers in marginal areas to reduce wheat area or shift to less water-intensive crops, the market will increasingly price in tighter 2026-27 supplies.
Trading & Price Outlook
- Short-term bias: Mildly bullish. Slow sowing and weak moisture underpin wheat prices, with limited downside as long as mandi levels remain near or above MSP.
- Millers/consumers: Consider advancing a portion of procurement for Q4 2026–Q1 2027 coverage while prices are still only moderately above MSP, but stagger purchases to retain flexibility should sowing conditions improve.
- Farmers: In well-irrigated zones, maintaining intended wheat area remains attractive given firm prices and policy support. In moisture-stressed areas, diversification into pulses or oilseeds may reduce agronomic and income risk.
- Traders: Monitor weekly rabi acreage data and reservoir updates closely; further confirmation of persistent sowing delays or crop-switching would justify a stronger bullish stance.

work-careers-bfd07d6e46.fulltext: Hyderabad: While AI has become a buzzword across the global tech industry and is being linked to layoffs, Global Capability Centres (GCCs) in India appears to be embracing the shift. For instance, about 80% of the portfolio customers of ANSR, a global GCC enabler, are building AI Centres of Excellence. . “In the last three months, more than 2,400 specialists were hired into AI-related roles, along with over 120 global leaders, including Global Heads of AI who now lead from their GCCs in India,” ANSR Co-founder Vikram Ahuja told reporters here. . He said AI and specialised capabilities will drive the next phase of GCC growth in India, and noted that GCCs are increasingly taking responsibility for building products, deploying AI and shaping engineering and business capabilities. .LTM launches 'GCC Origin' unit to expand GCC operations in India. “ANSR’s Talent Trends in GCCs in India 2026 analysis, based on more than 5,000 live openings and over 20,000 roles hired, found that nearly two-thirds of new GCC roles require AI skills. Demand for AI-related talent has grown by about 45% YoY. AI expertise is also becoming a baseline requirement in established functions such as software development, product management, finance, cybersecurity and operations,” Ahuja added. . Talent expectations . Talent500, ANSR’s talent platform with a community of 3.6 million professionals, surveyed 1,118 tech, product and data professionals across India for its What Talent Wants 2026 report, released earlier this month. It found that 71% of respondents consider hands-on AI upskilling important, but only 29% say their employer provides it, the widest gap between expectation and delivery among the six areas tested. . Career clarity matters just as much, as 87% said defined career-growth information is very important, and 79% would drop an application or decline an offer if there is no clear career path or growth story. . Hyderabad’s growing role . Hyderabad has been strengthening its position in India’s GCC ecosystem as global enterprises expand beyond traditional delivery operations to build specialised capabilities in AI, product engineering, data and innovation. ANSR, which has established more than 250 GCCs, has set up about 30% of them in Hyderabad. . ANSR has helped global enterprises set up and scale GCCs in the city, including FedEx, Bristol Myers Squibb, Advance Auto Parts, Marriott International, Inspire Brands, owner of Dunkin’ and Baskin-Robbins, Stolt-Nielsen and CIBC. The company sees Hyderabad as a multifunctional GCC hub, where enterprises can run technology, analytics, finance, operations and shared services from a single location. Bengaluru remains the stronghold for engineering, product development and R&D, Ahuja added. . An ANSR report noted that Hyderabad has achieved operational parity with established hubs such as Bengaluru, attracting 70 new enterprise capability centres in the 2025 fiscal alone. Strong infrastructure, a highly-skilled workforce and a business-friendly environment have driven this growth. ANSR Chief Market Officer Smitha Hemmigae said the Telangana Government’s proactive policies have further strengthened the city’s appeal as a GCC destination. .Rising security investment alone is not enough in AI era, study finds. A recent FICCI report puts Hyderabad at more than 515 GCCs, employing over three lakh professionals as of March 2026, close to a fifth of India’s GCC base. GCC office leasing in the city rose from about 1.9 million sq ft in 2021 to 4.5 million sq ft in 2025, with a further 3.05 million sq ft absorbed in the first half of 2026. . Rise of nano GCCs . A new feature of the current growth phase is the rise of “nano GCCs”, which are smaller, specialised capability centres set up by mid-market enterprises, PE-backed businesses and newer global companies. Alongside large multinationals, these firms use GCCs to access specialised talent, accelerate product development and build global operating capability without the scale traditionally associated with large captive centres. . “The GCC is no longer a model reserved for the largest enterprises. Mid-market and PE-backed companies are building focused, specialised centres, often starting small and scaling as the mandate grows. We see it in the doubling of our pipeline from PE partners and PE-backed companies, and it is changing what a GCC looks like,” Ahuja said.

other-interests-05f38e9dee.headline: An exclusive conversation with the developer of REA, the viral AI reverse engineering tool
other-interests-05f38e9dee.fulltext:
Buy a new car, and you’re free to repaint the exterior or add new wheels. But you aren’t supposed to edit the code controlling the dash display and other electronics. Once software is packaged up and shipped, it’s meant to stay the way the manufacturer intended it.
Morluto, a software engineer who spoke with Scientific American on the condition that he remain pseudonymous, took that as a challenge. His tool, Reverse Engineer Anything, or REA, lets artificial intelligence agents pull apart programs and reconstitute them to their users’ liking.
His interest began with game decompilation, a corner of reverse engineering in which fans painstakingly rebuild the code of video games. Such work has taken years without AI assistance. Now Morluto—whose name comes from an old video gaming alias—sees much broader uses. REA’s Discord community includes examples of people modifying everything from printers to televisions. The project has more than 400,000 stars on GitHub, a rough gauge of its popularity.
On supporting science journalism
