“We’ve gotten used to the fact that software is all around us, but none of it is anything that we can influence,” he says. He hopes AI-enabled reverse engineering could fix this: “If code is magic, then we are all capable of it,” Morluto says.
For decades, software makers have enjoyed a sense of security through tedium: taking apart a compiled program was such a grind that few people bothered. But the packaging also kept us out of the guts of our own gadgets. If anyone with a ChatGPT subscription or an open-weight model can hand off that work, control over a device tilts toward whoever’s curious to look inside—no matter their intentions. “This is going to pose a crisis for trade secret and copyright law,” says James Grimmelmann, a law professor at Cornell Tech.
Morluto sees this as a natural progression in the relationship between people and the technology they use. Throughout our conversation, he kept invoking tech founders who shaped his work—Apple’s Steve Jobs, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Y Combinator’s Paul Graham. “A lot of the creators in the past,” he says, “were all hackers and tinkerers, experimenters growing up.” He believes REA can turn its users into that kind of creator. “You are capable not just of magic but of creating beautiful things,” Morluto says.
In his view, tech has become an industry full of walled gardens, and thanks to AI, “their walls were not as robust as they had thought.”
Those walls come from the way software is bundled into executable programs. Before a program can run, the code people write in a programming language such as Python has to be translated, or compiled, into binary, a sequence of 1’s and 0’s that actually tells the computer what to do. Reverse engineering software involves running that translation backward, turning binary back into code a person can read in the process of decompilation.
Reverse engineers have long done this with tools such as Ghidra, a program the U.S. National Security Agency developed as part of its cybersecurity efforts. REA provides the pipelines that let an AI agent orchestrate Ghidra and other programs on its own.
"Reverse engineering is a little bit like pattern matching," says Morluto. "AI has extremely strong reasoning and pattern matching skills."
Before 2026 decompilation was the domain of a select few experts, according to Zion Basque, an assistant professor at the University of Georgia, who studies reverse engineering. Now, he says, nearly anyone can play. His research group developed Kuna, one of the decompilers REA can equip AI agents with. The kinds of reverse engineering he sees people doing with REA could have been done before, just never at this scale. “I haven’t seen what the limits of this are yet,” he says.
Done by hand, that kind of work would take experts months, if they managed it at all, according to Grimmelmann. Now the limit, he says, is what you can afford. “If you have the tokens, you can set it loose on almost any piece of software,” he says.
For some corners of the software industry, that’s an existential problem that the law cannot easily patch. Copyright protects a program’s code, Grimmelmann says, but not the algorithms and ideas the code implements. “This opens up a whole world of mods and remixes and interoperable new clients that really reduce the lead time people get from deploying software,” he says.
REA isn’t the only thing eating into that head start. In early October Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 helped a developer build open-source clones of Adobe’s Creative Cloud programs, which are known for their tight controls and steep prices.
Joey Castillo, an open-source developer and technologist in residence at Cornell Tech, went after something smaller. He has reverse engineered various tools in the past, but his first brush with using AI to do it came when he tried to modify a smart ring he had bought in Shenzhen, China. He was impressed that the AI model could reverse engineer the ring and teach him at the same time. “I learned a lot just by watching Claude work,” he says.
The desire to tinker comes from wanting to take control of the things you buy, according to Castillo. “I bought this object, and it’s being gatekept from me,” he says. “Now I’m going to have the power to make it do what I want.”
Some of those gates serve an important purpose, though. Much as AI is proving adept at breaking into security systems, it is also very good at breaking things like digital rights management and the protected firmware baked into devices.
Projects like REA may also make it too easy for amateurs to gain a sort of synthetic expertise. Castillo and his open-source friends worry about people digging around in devices they don’t fully understand. “This is all going to be very fun and games until someone vibe codes firmware and it causes the battery to catch fire midflight,” Castillo says. He doubts AI models have the foresight that reverse engineering experts bring to deciding which modifications to make because AI “can only ‘yes, and.’ It can’t ‘no, but.’”
Since our first conversation with Morluto, some social media users have reported OpenAI and Anthropic banning or blocking their use of REA. In a reply on X, an OpenAI researcher called the block on reverse engineering “mostly accidental.”
Morluto isn’t worried. If anything, he says, the “fiasco” just brings more attention to the project and to the kind of discovery he was aiming for. “That’s the core of Reverse Engineer Anything,” he says. “It’s a road that leads you to question what it is that you want.”
Accidental or not, such obstacles are unlikely to stop people who really want to reverse engineer their devices. Castillo already has a fallback in GLM-5.3, an open-weight model from the Chinese company Z.ai. Once it’s downloaded, no one can take it away. “If Anthropic and OpenAI decide they’re going to ban my account for reverse engineering, I’m going to fire up GLM-5.3 and reverse engineer the smart ring,” he says, “because I think it’s really cool to make this thing do what I wanted.”

longform-47e0ed2b86.headline: The Internet Might Need to Be Rebuilt From Scratch
longform-47e0ed2b86.fulltext:
AI hacking swarms are poking holes across the internet at such a rate that some cybersecurity professionals have dubbed this month “Black October.” The AI-cybersecurity professional Alex Stamos argues that it’s time to be proactive rather than reactive, and that might mean rewriting the code for the internet in newer programming languages that could make all of our online systems and personal information safer. He joins the Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel to explain why that’s not as big of a deal as it sounds, and how we can all protect ourselves in the meantime.
Alex Stamos: What we have to do, as people who work in cybersecurity, is: We have to shorten the Dark Age. We need to make sure the Library of Alexandria doesn’t burn, right? We have to do everything possible to make this as short as possible. And from my perspective, the best way to do that is to be proactive, not reactive, here. And to be proactive we can’t just wait for these bad things to happen; we have to intentionally re-architect things.
Charlie Warzel: It’s late October. There’s an upcoming election. There’s a World Series. There’s this endless string of bracing news events. But there’s another crisis looming as well. The digital infrastructure that powers our entire on- and offline lives is, according to the people who protect it, more vulnerable than ever. The internet as we know it is a very fragile ecosystem. So much of it is built off of code that’s written by humans—that is, by nature, full of flaws or bugs. Some of our critical digital infrastructure, it’s built off of decades-old technology that’s running on ancient code languages.
The internet is a marvel. But it is also, like any massive human endeavor, imperfect and full of vulnerabilities. One way to look at the history of cybersecurity is as a race between people who are looking to exploit all those vulnerabilities and the people who can fortify our systems and keep them secure.
But in recent months, AI has threatened to change the dynamics of that race. AI agents—which are cheap, relentless, and highly capable hacker armies—are proving excellent at finding vulnerabilities in code. Sometimes, oftentimes, in places that humans had never thought to look. And the result has been this series of high-profile cybersecurity incidents, each one adding to this feeling that we’ve entered a new era.
The rate of disclosures of incidents has been so intense that in recent weeks, cybersecurity professionals are referring to this month as Black October. Last week, the public found out that AI agents found vulnerability in PHP, which is a coding language that affects 70 percent of the internet, that could allow hackers to gain access to almost any server. On top of PHP, there have been disclosures in major software products like Node.js, which is software that’s used across countless important webpages and services on the internet. This is stuff that powers everything from supply chains to health-care companies.
And the fear is that what we are seeing here is not some kind of aberration, but the beginning of this new normal—this period of time where everything from our power grids to our personal data may be uniquely vulnerable.
And so I wanted to understand exactly how unprecedented this Black October moment really is, and what it means for the state of the internet and the possibilities of catastrophic events in the future. Alex Stamos is the chief information security officer at the AI company Cognition, and the former chief security officer at Facebook. He is not only on the forefront of this current crisis, but he’s also somebody who understands how massive digital organizations respond to the demands of an increasingly insecure internet.
Warzel: So we’re in the middle of what feels right now like this explosion of either AI-powered hacks or cybersecurity disclosures. Right now, people in your industry, and colloquially on places like X are referring to it as Black October. Pretty ominous. Can you walk me through what has changed fundamentally in the last two weeks?
Stamos: Yeah. So we’re just kind of—this has honestly been a slow burn. But what’s been really interesting in this month is that finally attackers are getting the benefit from AI; where they have the ability to use AI to automate what we call kill chains. So you know, this is a term we have stolen from the military—where, when the military says “kill chain,” they mean to actually kill something. In the cyber world, those are the steps you take to break into a network and to do something.
And traditionally, you could automate some parts of a kill chain. But there’s often human steps. And just in the last several months, we’ve gotten to the point of where AI models—and especially the open-weight models, the models that you can run locally on hardware you run yourself, and even commodity hardware like these new Mac Studios that you can buy—are good enough that basically every step of the kill chain can be completely automated with AI. And so that has really changed the game here—where you can get rid of any human bottleneck. And that has completely changed the economics and the speed at which attackers can move.
Warzel: So I’ve heard of this being talked about as a “disclosure wave,” meaning that it’s a disclosure of potential vulnerabilities and not a wave of attacks. But what’s the truth to that?
Stamos: Yeah, I don’t think that’s true. We’ve actually had a wave of attacks, but it’s way before this October. We’ve had a building wave of attacks over the last year or so as attackers have automated their kill chains. There’s a good thing happening, which is—these vulnerabilities have existed for decades, right? We have, you know, years and years and years of human-written code that is not reliable, that is not safe. That is often written in languages that are not what we call memory safe and type safe, that are written in computer languages that were not fundamentally easy to write safe code in. Languages like C and C++.
And unfortunately, it turns out that human beings writing code in those languages—it’s very hard to make systems that are safe in the presence of these superhuman bug-finders. And so what’s happening is we are now burning through all of these bugs that were written over two decades, and they are being found and discovered and patched. But the problem is, once those patches are released, actually getting them fixed in the wild takes a while. And so bad guys have a window during which they can then exploit them. And over the last year, we have seen that exploitation happening. Sometimes manually, and more and more automatically.
And so yes—we have seen waves and waves of exploitation. It’s not being covered as much, but it is extremely hard if you have a security emergency on a Friday evening. And it’s often on a Friday evening; unfortunately, that’s how it often seems to work out. It is very hard to get professional incident responders on the phone, because everybody is booked up pretty far out right now.
Warzel: So all of this news, as an outsider, is really bracing to just see come across the timeline. I don’t think it’s very clear for a lot of us without the expertise to evaluate some of these claims.
The one that I saw the other day that I wanna bring up here is the reports that the cloud service from Japan’s GMO Internet Group, which is used also by financial traders, had been hacked. And in one report that I saw circulating, the CEO of GMO suggested that the internet as we know it could be on the verge of collapse due to this pressure.
When we hear something like that, how are we supposed to evaluate that kind of claim? What is the state of the internet right now?
Stamos: Oh, so to say the internet is going to collapse, I think, is hyperbole. The fundamental infrastructure of the internet is holding up fine, right? Like the internet—the routers, the switches—there have been bugs in the fundamental systems that move traffic, but those have been fixed.
I think what is happening, however, is we have lived through a period where you have been able to assume that if you use a service, that your data is going to be safe. That assumption was never correct, it turns out. Right? The systems were never safe. It’s just that we lacked the number of skilled attackers to take advantage of the fundamental insecurity of these systems.
And what is happening now is the bugs are being found. Sometimes by the bad guys, often by the good guys. But in the period in which it takes for the bugs to be fixed, the bad guys have an opportunity to take advantage of that period of time, of that lag of fixing them. And then the bad guys—the skill sets. You know, I don’t know if you’re an English soccer/football fan, but everybody gets this metaphor now ’cause they watch Ted Lasso. But you know, right, so the English football leagues—if you do really well, you get sent up, right? If you do poorly, you get relegated; you get sent down.
Well, what’s happening is: Every attacker is now getting sent up a league, right? And so you know, it used to be the Premier League was just a handful of really big countries—so the United States and our allies—called the Five Eyes. So the United States, the U.K., Canada, Australia, New Zealand, is called the Five Eyes. Russia, China, Israel, a couple other Western nations were up there at the top. And then you had the next tier—which was like Iran, North Korea, a couple other second-tier countries. And then you had the really good independent professional commercial groups.
And what’s happening is everybody’s going up a league, because of AI. Which in some ways is bad for the people at the top, because they’re losing their premier status. Now, a 19-year-old in St. Petersburg can do that with a M5 Mac Ultra. That’s kind of—and that’s really crazy.

That everyone is elevated; everyone has these skills they didn’t have. But if people without even real basic knowledge of these systems or skills can do this, how is this sustainable for, you know, cybersecurity?

longform-9eab603604.headline: In praise of the dilettante
longform-9eab603604.fulltext:
Listen to this essay
21 minute listen
Why, of all people, defend the dilettante? An amateur at best, a flighty rascal at worst: why take an interest in someone whose own interests are never more than a passing hobby? These are serious times – why take seriously someone for whom nothing is serious?
Merriam-Webster defines the dilettante as ‘a person having a superficial interest in an art or a branch of knowledge’. Encyclopedia.com calls the dilettante someone who cultivates an interest ‘without real commitment or knowledge’. Cambridge settles for someone whose understanding ‘is not very deep or serious’. Collins gives us someone who ‘seems interested in a subject … but does not really know very much about it’. None of it is flattering.
Clearly, the dilettante is no aspirational character. No university markets itself as training the next generation of dilettantes; no magazine runs a ‘dilettante of the year’ issue (except, perhaps, for the excellent Idler publication). He – for the dilettante is, historically and in popular imagination, so often a ‘he’ – is in essence an amateur, a role defined by wide interests and narrow expertise.
Such is the reputation of the dilettante, assigned and maintained by a culture that treats a single-minded devotion to one pursuit as the only route to a meaningful life. Pick something and stick with it, we are told. It’s not so much an explicit campaign against dilettantism I’m challenging, but rather the diffuse yet relentless pressure to narrow one’s interests, to specialise, to gain expertise, to forgo breadth for the sake of depth. We hear it in the barrage of imperatives to follow your dreams or find your passion uttered at graduation speeches, in self-help guides, and similarly corporate-sounding pep talks. Under this scheme, the specialist is the hero and the dilettante is but a cautionary tale: the person who never committed, never finished, never got good enough at any one thing.
But what if the scheme has it backwards? What if the dilettante’s perpetual movement from one thing to another is not a failure of nerve but a different and defensible way of being, one whose exploratory zeal turns out to be just what a hyper-specialised, over-optimised and all-too-serious world needs most? Then the dilettante would turn out to be not a capricious buffoon but a kind of modern anti-hero. That, I argue, is a dilettantism worth defending.
First, let’s consider how ‘dilettante’ relates to some of its conceptual cousins: the amateur, the dabbler, the jack-of-all-trades, etc. First, the dilettante is by nature an amateur, ie, a non-expert, a non-professional. But amateurism is a necessary though not sufficient condition of dilettantism. Anyone can be an amateur at any particular thing: woodworking, birdwatching, astronomy, etc. The dilettante’s amateurism is wide-ranging over several interests, and tends to orient around the production and/or appreciation of art and beauty. Like the jack-of-all-trades, the dilettante is a multi-dimensional amateur. But the dilettante’s amateurism is typically of the aesthetic variety.
Further, the dilettante is no dabbler. The dabbler scratches the surface of interests, whereas the dilettante, I argue, can and does go deep – without, however, anchoring a sense of self in any one interest. This also sets the dilettante apart from the flâneur, Charles Baudelaire’s urban wanderer strolling through the city’s offerings, sampling everything, invested in none of it. The dilettante is deeply engaged in interests, and more an active participant than a passive spectator.
The term originally referred to someone who pursues an interest, particularly an artistic one, for the sake of ‘delight’
In this respect, the concept is closest in spirit to the ‘Renaissance man’, minus the gender specification and historical context. The dilettante is one who is moved by enjoyment rather than necessity, professional obligation or the pursuit of credentials, and who purposefully cultivates a plurality of distinct, often aesthetic interests beyond mere surface familiarity.
One reason to defend the dilettante, then, is for lexicological justice. The term has been unfairly burdened with an overly negative connotation. It wasn’t always this way. From the Baroque-era Italian dilettante, the term originally referred to someone who pursues an interest, particularly an artistic one, for the sake of pleasure, or ‘delight’. Even as the term evolved, it stayed largely neutral, distinguishing enthusiasts from professionals in a given practice. The pejorative connotation familiar to us today is more recent, shaped by what I’ll call a ‘deficiency’ model, in which amateurism is viewed negatively as a lack of something: skill, seriousness, focus, expertise. This is the meaning ascribed by cultural gatekeepers like Theodor Adorno, who in 1929 dismissed the dilettante as one ‘unable to establish any standards’.
The more important aim, however, is to show dilettantism as a way of living that offers more than we might think. It is a life liberated from specialisation, instrumentalisation and meritocratic bean-counting, as well as from a Protestant work ethic that is suspicious of pleasure for pleasure’s sake. Arguments denigrating specialisation in education and vocation are well known, as are those championing well-roundedness and the virtues of the liberal arts. Though similar in spirit, this defence of dilettantism is less about the purpose or outcomes of academic or professional life and more about making the mental switch away from the socially conditioned pressure to find your thing and stick with it to an open and exploratory pursuit of pluralistic interests. Reclaiming this sense of joyful experimentalism is intended to show dilettantism as a mode of abundance rather than deficiency.
A good place to start is the essay ‘On Dilettantism’ (1799) by J W von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller. This fragmentary, never-completed project by the literary dream-team of Weimar-era Germany paints a deeply ambivalent portrait of dilettantism, praising the dilettante over here for ‘cultivat[ing] something serious in man’ and condemning him over there as a ‘plagiarist’ and a ‘bungler’. Viewed retrospectively, however, its almost scientific treatment of the ‘advantages’ (Nutzen) and ‘disadvantages’ or ‘harms’ (Schaden) of dilettantism helps give a clear-eyed view of the potential virtues and vices of dilettantism today.
Crucially, Goethe and Schiller’s analysis is squarely situated in the cultural context of Weimar classicism. This means that, first, the question of the dilettante arises (as it does in its original Italian usage) exclusively in relation to the arts. They treat the dilettante as a distinctly aesthetic figure, ‘a lover of the arts who wishes not only to contemplate and enjoy them, but also to participate in their production.’ This aesthetic dimension has (regrettably, I think) faded from the meaning of ‘dilettante’ over time. But nor does it need to be narrowly inscribed in 18th-century anxieties about who can and cannot properly be called an artist. Artistic engagement isn’t essential to dilettantism. But it is worth reasserting, maybe even foregrounding, the sense in which the ‘delight’ of dilettantism involves, to some extent, the experience of aesthetic pleasure, broadly understood. The dilettante, that is, pursues what Søren Kierkegaard calls an ‘aesthetic life’: the ongoing, everyday activity of observing, valuing, and participating in art and beauty.
The dilettante is comfortable in the garb of an amateur. For the dilettante, every night is karaoke night
Though rooted in classicist aestheticism, some of Goethe and Schiller’s criticism of the dilettante still resonates today. They worry, for example, that the dilettante ‘jumps over the steps’, gliding too glibly through the creative process and claiming victory too early. There’s something to this. Similar to Oscar Wilde’s concern about the ‘sentimentalist’ in his 1897 epistolary essay, De Profundis, who ‘desires to have the luxury of an emotion without paying for it’, the authors voice a reasonable objection to those willing to cut the line in chasing laurels. Progress is earned through practice, and those of us who have put in the work are right to protect it, as any trained therapist, frustrated with the quackery that passes for therapy on YouTube and TikTok, will gladly testify.
But due to their idealisation of the ‘true artist’ as a manifester of Truth and Beauty, Goethe and Schiller cannot help but view the dilettante as lacking in both aim and ability. To be fair, no practice is a total free-for-all, and some practices are less permissive of dilettantism than others (who wants to live in a house built by a dilettante architect?). But the notion that the dilettante tries and fails to follow the ‘true objective rules’ of art and beauty the way legit artists do rests on outdated and Eurocentric assumptions about what both artists and dilettantes are actually up to. In other words, take away the neo-classicist presumption, and suddenly the dilettante appears less like an imitator and more like a liberated creator. It’s not that the dilettante falls short in any given practice but, rather, has a different orientation toward it. Indeed, an overly goal-oriented attitude, especially in the realm of pastimes and pleasures, cuts against the very spirit of dilettantism. Part of its appeal is its ethos of open-endedness, its willingness to do something for the sake of delight rather than achievement. The dilettante is comfortable in the garb of an amateur. For the dilettante, every night is karaoke night.
From our Germans, we glean a sense of where the dilettante goes wrong. But they can also help us make the corrective mental switch from seeing the dilettante as a wannabe practitioner to someone who chooses a more experimental, exploratory orientation toward a given practice.
The key to perceiving dilettantism as abundance instead of deficiency is to appreciate the sense of freedom it affords. It is, in the first place, a negative freedom, a freedom from the constraints that otherwise bind professional practitioners. More precisely, it is a freedom of mobility within a practice.
First, the dilettante has greater freedom to engage in a given practice. For Goethe and Schiller, one of the most important ‘advantages’ of dilettantism is that it ‘stimulates a certain taste for art, and extends it to where the artist would not be able to reach’. Generalising a bit, the point holds well beyond art: the dilettante can act as a liaison between expert and layperson, closing the gap between high practice and everyday curiosity, introducing otherwise cloistered practitioners to wider audiences and extending an invitation to anyone who might otherwise feel shut out.
A personal example. A few years ago, I joined Mountain Haulers, a cycling group that meets on Tuesday evenings for a ride through Asheville, North Carolina. It is a ‘no drop’ ride: cyclists wait at points along the way for everyone to catch up, however slow or struggling, and the first ride of the month is always a chill ride along the river. This openness sets the group apart from a cycling culture of notorious cliques of devotees clamouring to outdo each other’s worship of the sport. Welcoming the less-experienced and the less-committed seems a more genuine way of loving the thing you claim to love. If biking is your thing, surely you want more butts on bike seats. The dilettante cyclists who show up for Tuesday-night rides make cycling better.
The modern admonition to ‘stay in your lane’ stems from assumptions about the commitment required to claim an interest as one’s own
The further sense of the dilettante’s freedom involves mobility between different practices – a freedom from the barriers dividing them. The dilettante maintains a certain detachment, or intentional separation, between who one is and what one does, to live the life of a cultural iti

global-economics-c6608a9a56.headline: Tech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reports
global-economics-c6608a9a56.fulltext:
A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies drove US markets down by hundreds of billions of dollars Friday. In total, the decline has knocked nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
The S&P 500, the index of the 500 most valuable companies in the US, fell by more than 1% Friday, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. It was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the same month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell less.
More than $2tn in market value is set to be wiped from the Nasdaq 100 this month, as big tech earnings intensified investor scrutiny of whether the billions being poured into artificial intelligence can generate returns quickly enough.
The wipeout would amount to slightly more than SpaceX’s entire market value. The index has fallen more than 5.8% so far in October as the AI trade ran into turbulence, with hyperscalers Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon raising spending forecasts further as they race to expand AI infrastructure.
Intel tumbled nearly 30% and is flirting with its worst day since 1974, even though the chipmaker reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell far short of analysts’ expectations.
Amazon fell 1.8% after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. The company also disclosed that it had spent more this year than anticipated.
A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12%, wiping $500bn from its market capitalization, to its worst day on record after telling investors that it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring because of similar, mammoth investments in AI.
Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make AI investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI datacenters have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward.
Such losses overshadowed an otherwise mixed day for the rest of Wall Street, with the S&P 500 roughly evenly split between gainers and losers.
Expectations are high broadly for US companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

ISRO’s Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) lifted off for the twentieth time in the final minutes of Friday as it carried NVS-03, the latest entry in India’s NavIC series of satellites.
The rocket took off from the Second Launch Pad (SLP) at Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh and successfully injected the satellite into the intended Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO).
Over the next few days, NVS-03 will use its own propulsion systems to perform orbital manoeuvres and rise to the final Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO).

— ISRO (@isro) October 30, 2026
The NavIC series of satellites is intended to replace the ageing Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS) - India’s first generation of navigation satellites. A constellation of multiple navigation satellites will allow Indians to have a fully indigenous version of GPS.
The satellites, working in tandem, are designed to provide accurate Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) service to users in India as well as the region extending about 1500 km beyond the Indian landmass, which is its primary service area.
The successful injection of NVS-03, though a noteworthy milestone at this stage, does not guarantee full success and operational readiness, with the satellite now having to make the perilous orbital manoeuvres needed to rise to GEO. In fact, NVS-02, the previous iteration in the series, while successfully injected to GTO, was unable to move to the GEO orbit due to issues with its pyro valve.
This was the 20th mission for the three-stage GSLV rocket, with 14 successes, 4 failures, and 2 partial failures to date.
Speaking after the launch, ISRO Chairman said that the GSLV launch vehicle has now carried about 30 tons of spacecraft to date. He also added that the mission was the shortest turnaround in the history of the GSLV rocket, launching just 56 days after its previous mission.
“The NavIC constellation is a strategic asset that provides the nation with independent access to Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT). In addition to strategic capabilities, these satellites will also be used for civilian applications like tracking of vehicles and is important component of the one nation one time project

Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) will launch the navigation satellite NVS-03 aboard the GSLV-F18 rocket at 11:51 PM IST tonight. The liftoff will take place from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh.

indian-startups-c2d47ab1fd.headline: MeitY Floats New Privacy-Led Framework To Unlock Data For Training AI Models
indian-startups-c2d47ab1fd.fulltext: The IT ministry (MeitY) has proposed a consent-based framework to facilitate data sharing for training AI models in India. Called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI training, the framework aims to help startups, businesses and academic institutions access large-scale, India-specific datasets to develop AI models while protecting citizens' privacy and ensuring compliance with the DPDP Act. The DEPA for AI training also proposes a techno-legal architecture to enable organisations to collaborate on AI model training without directly transferring underlying datasets. With this, the ministry aims to foster access to datasets for researchers and businesses looking to train AI models. The guidelines have been formulated in collaboration with think tank iSPIRT. Explaining The New Proposed Framework The proposed architecture builds on India’s existing DEPA framework, which already supports consent-based data sharing through initiatives such as Account Aggregator. The new framework encompasses the following technical pillars: Confidential Clean Rooms: Secure computing environments where organisations can collaborate on data processing and AI model training without exposing the underlying datasets to one another Differential Privacy: A privacy-preserving technique used to ensure that individual-level information cannot be identified or extracted from an aggregate dataset Electronic Contracts: Machine-readable agreements that define and enforce data-sharing conditions, including permitted uses, data protection and security requirements Zero-Trust Security: An approach where every access request is authenticated and authorised, with encryption, continuous monitoring and auditing to protect data The proposed framework also defines key stakeholders for enabling safe sharing of data for training AI models: Training Data Providers (TDPs): Organisations that make their data accessible through the framework. For instance: banks, hospitals, government agencies Training Data Consumers (TDCs): Startups, enterprises, researchers and individuals seeking access to datasets to train AI models Data Collectives or Data Collabs: Intermediaries that aggregate, standardise, and organise data from various sources and define data-sharing policies and governance rules for participants Under the DEPA framework, TDPs would first register their datasets on a data exchange platform after anonymising and encrypting them. The datasets would then be tagged with metadata and cryptographic identifiers for traceability. TDCs can then request a dataset for their specific use cases, and an electronic contract system checks their requests against data-sharing policies and governance rules before granting access. Once access is given, the model is then trained within a secure data environment using differential privacy methods, ensuring that the raw data remains inaccessible to consumers. The framework also proposes that trained models must undergo independent checks for bias, fairness, security, safety and explainability. Only models that pass receive approval for pilot deployment and scaling. Even after deployment, the oversight will continue in the interest of long-term trust and accountability. In line with this, the framework will ensure that TDCs remain subject to continuous monitoring, periodic reviews, and traceability of the model’s outputs back to the data and contracts used in its training. Govt’s Focus On AI Governance The launch of the new DEPA framework for AI training comes soon after TRAI also released draft guidelines on the responsible use of AI in telecom networks and service delivery. The telecom regulator has sought inputs from stakeholders by November 27. As per TRAI, its draft guidelines are rooted in the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines. The centre had earlier released these guidelines to focus on fostering innovation and safe development and deployment of AI offerings, while mitigating risks posed by the technology. A few weeks ago, union IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw had also said that the centre will release a consultation paper for regulation on AI safety and security within a month. Earlier reports had also hinted that the Centre was looking at formulating a new framework for AI regulation.

world-9656678bad.headline: Experts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights case
world-9656678bad.fulltext:
Altering copyright law to allow AI companies to scrape music, books and journalism could trigger a constitutional breach, Coalition senators and the recording industry have warned, as they raise new fears it could open Australia to massive legal action and compensation claims from rights holders worldwide.
The attorney general’s department admitted it was “extremely alive” to the issue, and Australia’s leading constitutional expert, Anne Twomey, agreed there was “potentially” a concern – depending how legislation was drafted – that granting AI companies permission to scrape copyrighted material from the internet could amount to an acquisition of property by the government.
In a simmering debate centred on the same legal point as the movie The Castle, the question of acquiring property “on just terms” is emerging as a key concern amid furious lobbying from tech companies and rights holders ahead of a looming federal government announcement on AI.
“We could be liable for ‘just terms’ compensation for acquiring that property for every rights holder on Earth,” Ross Cadell, a Nationals senator, told Guardian Australia.
Michaelia Cash, the shadow attorney general, said the government should not “sell out Australian creators and rights holders in the rush to entice AI investment”.
Labor is mulling copyright changes in a suite of reforms around AI, including datacentres, online safety, workforce, energy and the economy. While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has promised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries are alarmed that AI companies have requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material.
Some AI companies have rejected making licensing agreements under existing copyright law, saying it was too difficult. Anthropic suggested an “opt-out” model which would allow it to scrape content unless a rightholder deployed digital protections signaling an objection.
A fresh concern being aired by sceptics and creatives is that any weakening of copyright to benefit AI could represent a breach of section 51 of the constitution, which allows the commonwealth to make laws about “the acquisition of property on just terms”.
“If they go ahead with an opt-out model, it does raise a real question of whether the government is acquiring the intellectual property rights of others,” said Cadell, a member of the federal parliamentary committee on AI.
“How we support property rights is core to this.”
A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said the government was “committed to supporting” creatives and pledged that “any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.
Anne Twomey, professor emerita of law at the University of Sydney, said the issue was exceedingly complex and noted no legislative proposal had been aired. She said numerous cases had come before the high court relating to copyright and acquisition of property, including about video games, cigarette plain packaging and cassette tapes, with varying outcomes.
Twomey expected the federal government would be hyperaware of such concerns, but said granting a new right to AI companies to use copyrighted material and diminishing the rights of copyright holders could “potentially” trigger constitutional issues.
“The high court has recognised a number of exceptions to section 51 … One would want to be quite confident before enacting the legislation about whether or not section 51 would apply,” Twomey told Guardian Australia.
She said any change allowing Australia to host AI companies training on international data could potentially create grounds for global rights holders to take legal action here.
Cadell told Guardian Australia he worried about such a development opening the federal government to liability for “the biggest compensation rights case in history”.
Cadell raised his concerns about the constitution in a committee hearing with the attorney general’s department on Friday, in which officials said they were conscious of those issues.
Officials did not directly answer when Cadell asked about international implications and liability for compensation to foreign rights holders.
Annabelle Herd, the CEO of the Australian Recording Industry Association, claimed any proposal to allow AI companies to scrape data was “clearly an acquisition of property”.
“It’s hard to imagine what kind of compensation would make up for the fact that they’re basically taking our right … and trading it away to the AI companies to then monetise themselves, and that appears to be a clear path to a constitutional challenge.”
Chris Maund, CEO of Mushroom Records, said current copyright law was working and that AI companies should use existing licensing arrangements, noting companies such as Spotify were already making AI-related deals.
He also raised concern about international ramifications were Australia to change copyright law, saying it would not only apply to Australian artists and copyright owners.
“The AI company could do their training here in Australia and circumvent the copyright laws that apply outside of Australia, and that’s why the international creative industries are watching this very closely,” he said.
Maund said international rights holder groups had been urging Labor not to weaken copyright law. Guardian Australia has provided submissions to the Joint Select Committee as a member of Australia’s wider rights holder community.
“The Australian government has been really great to the music industry, particularly Prime Minister Albanese and Tony Burke. They’ve set up Creative Music Australia, which companies like us and our artists have done very well out of, but it feels like they’re out of step with artists and copyright owners on this point,” he said.
Cash said the Coalition welcomed the benefits of AI and wanted investment, but also raised the constitutional concern.
“That is the prime minister’s own test, and the government should be held to it,” she said of compensation to rights holders.
“The constitutional question of property rights and their acquisition on just terms is also a live issue we will be examining depending on what the government puts forward.”
Cadell said while AI had benefits, he worried about its risks.
“There’s lots of talk about what the benefits may be and what may happen. But if we take these rights away, we know what will happen,” Cadell said.
“I don’t want to hurt people for a ‘may’.”

india-deep-tech-f445ed73eb.headline: DRDO showcases indigenous semiconductor technologies, leads session on next-generation chips at ESTIC 2026
india-deep-tech-f445ed73eb.fulltext:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) led a thematic session on ‘Semiconductors & Next-Generation Chips’ and showcased its advanced indigenous technologies at the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC) 2026, held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, from October 27 to 29.
The conclave, themed ‘Creative Minds, Catalysing Science, Empowering Society’, was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and jointly organised by 12 ministries/departments under the guidance of the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India.
The event brought together Nobel Laureates, global experts, policymakers and emerging leaders to showcase cutting-edge research, deep-tech breakthroughs and developments in science and technology, said a press release by the Ministry of Defence.
DRDO leads session on semiconductors and next-generation chips
As one of the key organisers, DRDO led the thematic session on ‘Semiconductors & Next-Generation Chips’. Distinguished Scientist and Director General, Electronics and Communication Systems (ECS), Dr BK Das, chaired the session, which brought together eminent representatives from industry, academia, the indigenous chip-development ecosystem and defence electronics.
A panel discussion, moderated by Dr BK Das, was also organised as part of the session. Distinguished Scientist and Director General (Micro Electronic Devices, Computational Systems & Cyber Systems), Dr Sheena Rani, was among the panellists.
The discussions explored emerging developments in semiconductor technologies, purpose-built Artificial Intelligence (AI) System-on-Chips (SoCs), intelligence at the silicon edge and the evolving microprocessor landscape.
The session also highlighted DRDO’s evolving role in enabling industries and start-ups to develop game-changing solutions, accelerate next-generation chip design and strengthen indigenous core technologies.
Indigenous technologies showcased at DRDO outreach stall
The DRDO Outreach Stall showcased key initiatives, achievements, research programmes and contributions of the Ministry of Defence towards science, technology and innovation.
The exhibits included a range of indigenous technologies developed by DRDO laboratories, such as advanced communication systems, quantum technology prototypes, extreme-cold-weather clothing, PRABALA female full-body protector, passive and powered exoskeletons, portable hybrid energy management systems, high-power pulse laser diodes and scramjet engine technology.
DRDO also participated in the Thematic and Departmental Exhibitions at the conclave.
MMICs and infrared technologies on display
At the thematic exhibition on ‘Semiconductors and Next-Generation Chips’, DRDO showcased its achievements in two critical semiconductor technology domains — Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuits (MMICs) and Infrared Focal Plane Arrays (IRFPAs), developed by the Solid State Physics Laboratory (SSPL), Delhi.
Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) and Gallium Nitride (GaN)-based MMICs, along with Multi-Chip Modules (MCMs), displayed at the exhibition, have been employed in several strategic missions. These technologies serve as essential building blocks for advanced radar systems and Electronic Warfare (EW) applications.
The IRFPAs serve as the sensing elements or ‘eyes’ of tactical missiles, enabling target detection and tracking during the terminal phase through Imaging Infrared (IIR) seekers.
The exhibits covered a broad range of infrared technologies, including Short-Wave Infrared (SWIR), Mid-Wave Infrared (MWIR) and Long-Wave Infrared (LWIR), demonstrating DRDO’s indigenous capabilities in advanced semiconductor technologies.
Other notable DRDO exhibits included scramjet engine technology and neuromorphic accelerators, highlighting developments in complex and emerging technological domains. The exhibition also featured advanced communication systems, Quantum Random Number Generators (QRNGs), protective equipment, exoskeletons, portable hybrid energy management systems, Photonic Integrated Circuits (PICs) and laser proximity sensors.
Semiconductor self-reliance key to Viksit Bharat 2047
Semiconductor technology is a critical enabler of national sovereignty, economic strength and digital security. It plays a pivotal role in advancing the vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047 and Aatmanirbhar Bharat by strengthening indigenous technological capabilities.
From communication devices and advanced sensing systems to sophisticated defence platforms, semiconductor chips determine the performance, efficiency and reliability of modern technologies.
Beyond chip manufacturing, technological self-reliance requires comprehensive capabilities in chip design, fabrication, testing, industrial-scale production and resilient supply chains.
India aspires to emerge as a globally competitive, dependable and technologically self-reliant semiconductor powerhouse by 2047, with leadership in selected next-generation chip technologies. The vision encompasses developing a vibrant and sustainable semiconductor ecosystem, generating high-value employment opportunities and delivering inclusive societal benefits.
Over the years, India’s strategic defence laboratories and specialised semiconductor foundries, including SSPL, Gallium Arsenide Enabling Technology Centre (GAETEC), Semiconductor Technology and Applied Research Centre (STARC) and Semiconductor Laboratory (SCL), have developed specialised competencies in Gallium Arsenide (GaAs), Gallium Nitride (GaN), Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) and mature silicon process technologies.

indian-startups-c0d8063021.headline: Atomberg gets SEBI nod for proposed IPO
indian-startups-c0d8063021.fulltext:
Consumer appliances maker Atomberg Technologies has received approval from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) for its proposed initial public offering (IPO).
The IPO comprises a fresh issue of equity shares worth up to Rs 450 crore and an offer for sale (OFS) of 7.65 crore shares by existing shareholders. The company is yet to announce the price band and timeline for the issue.
Atomberg plans to use Rs 90 crore from the fresh issue proceeds to repay or prepay its borrowings. It will allocate Rs 150 crore towards brand awareness and performance marketing activities, while another Rs 100 crore will be used for research and development (R&D). The remaining amount will go towards general corporate purposes.
Founded in 2012 by Manoj Meena, who was joined by Sibabrata Das as co-founder in 2013, Atomberg initially focused on energy-efficient ceiling fans. It has since expanded its portfolio to include mixer grinders, water purifiers, cold-pressed juicers and other consumer appliances.
Apart from its consumer appliance business, the company also manufactures and supplies proprietary motors, controllers and other components to enterprise customers such as Voltas, Godrej and Blue Star through its subsidiary, Atomberg Innovations.
On the financial front, Atomberg's revenue from operations increased 34.8% to Rs 1,293.77 crore in FY26 from Rs 959.51 crore in FY25. However, its adjusted EBITDA declined to Rs 37.12 crore during the fiscal year from Rs 51.35 crore in FY25. The company reported a loss of Rs 148.88 crore in FY26, narrowing from Rs 199.08 crore in FY24.
Atomberg has also seen partial exits by existing investors ahead of its proposed listing. A91 Partners, which has backed the company since 2019, has sold shares worth around Rs 445 crore while retaining a 21% stake, according to the company's IPO disclosures.
ICICI Securities, Avendus Capital and IIFL Capital Services are the book-running lead managers to the issue.

health-tech-6f4cbad9c8.headline: Drug Regulators Order Sun Pharma to Halt Eye-Care Production at Assam Plant Over Quality Lapses
health-tech-6f4cbad9c8.fulltext:
Indian pharmaceutical major Sun Pharmaceutical Industries has been directed to halt the manufacture, sale and distribution of ophthalmic products produced at its facility in Assam after drug regulators identified shortcomings in its quality-management system.
According to documents reviewed by Reuters, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) and the Office of the Drugs Controller, Assam, issued the shutdown order on 20 August 2026. The action followed a joint inspection of the facility and an earlier show-cause notice dated 10 August.
Editorial Insight
Key Highlights
Important points readers should notice.
Issue/Event: Drug regulators ordered a halt to ophthalmic-product manufacturing, sale and distribution linked to Sun Pharma's Assam facility.
Location: India.
Authority/Organisation: Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) and the Office of the Drugs Controller, Assam.
Action Taken: Regulators issued a shutdown order on 20 August 2026 after a joint inspection and an unsatisfactory response to a show-cause notice; the company's compliance report is under review.
Impact: Ophthalmic production at the facility cannot resume until regulators accept the compliance response; the full contamination status and patient impact of the recalled batches remain unclear.
Regulators were reportedly dissatisfied with the company's response to the notice concerning quality-management failures. The company cannot resume ophthalmic production at the facility until its compliance report is reviewed and considered satisfactory by the authorities.
The regulatory action followed Sun Pharma's voluntary withdrawal of around 11 ophthalmology brands in July 2026. The company had described the withdrawal as a precautionary measure.
Regulators also sought further information concerning 332 batches of ophthalmic suspension products. These are liquid medicines used to treat various eye conditions. Reuters reported that it could not independently establish whether the 332 batches referred exclusively to the 11 recalled brands or included additional products.
Editorial Analysis
Why This Matters
Eye drops and other ophthalmic medicines require stringent quality controls because they are applied directly to the eye. Manufacturing failures involving sterile products can raise patient-safety concerns and require prompt regulatory scrutiny. The case also highlights the importance of transparent product-recall procedures, reliable batch tracking and effective communication between manufacturers, doctors, distributors and regulators. For patients, it is important to distinguish between products withdrawn from the market and other medicines that may have been manufactured at different facilities. A recall affecting selected products does not automatically mean that every medicine made by the company is affected.
Sun Pharma has submitted a compliance report, which was under regulatory review at the time of Reuters' report. The company did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Assam facility and the recall.
The wider safety picture requires careful distinction. The All India Ophthalmological Society had earlier raised concerns about possible contamination in certain batches of Predmet eye drops. An association representative told Reuters that infections had been reported among some patients who used the product and that testing of sealed bottles had found contamination. This does not establish that every recalled product or every affected batch was contaminated.
It also remains unclear whether all the recalled products were exported from India or whether patients experienced adverse effects linked to the wider recall.
